newsitem.title: GERMANY: Air India holds ex-Germany rates stable.
newsitem.headline: Air India holds ex-Germany rates stable.

text.p: Air India said it will keep official ex-Germany air cargo rates stable this autumn but it will try to raise ad-hoc prices.

The airline's cargo sales manager Germany, Ruediger Brasche, told Reuters in an interview that the market would not accept higher Germany to India rates, at a time of increasing competition and low growth.
But general market rates could rise through the loss of Air India's four times a week ex-Brussels freighter service with 150 tonnes capacity, he said.
"Our standard rates will remain the same. A general price rise cannot be put through on the market but we will try to raise prices in the ad hoc market," Brasche said.
"We will try to increase rates slightly because of the reduction in capacity and hope we can get back in November to last year's levels," he added.

Air India would have less capacity this autumn compared to 12 months previously because of the loss of the Brussels freighter and the sharing of ex-Frankfurt combi aircraft capacity with Paris, Brasche noted.
"If we take 150 tonnes out of the market, then perhaps rates on the eastbound sector will improve," he added.
Prices ex-Germany to India have fallen as low as 1.30 marks per kilo, with spot rates often undercutting this price, Brasche said.

Air India is achieving a load factor of up to 90 percent at present on its combi flights to India and expects to achieve about 4,500 tonnes total cargo exports from Germany in 1996, compared to some 6,000 tonnes last year, he said.
Demand in Germany for India remains strong but growth is low and competition is rising, he noted.
Brasche estimated Air India's share of the Germany to India market has fallen from 25 percent last year to 15 percent in 1996.
Competition in Europe is increasing rapidly with the launch of Lufthansa Cargo India, a joint venture between Lufthansa Cargo AG and Indian trading company Hinduja Group, he said.
KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Air France and Alitalia have all increased ex-Europe capacity and are gaining market share, he added.
About 80 percent of Air India's ex-Frankfurt freight is generated in Germany and the remainder is trucked from Scandinavia, the Netherlands and other neighbouring countries, Brasche said.
The airline flies up to 70 percent of its ex-Germany cargo to Bombay and Delhi, although higher rates can be achieved to destinations such as Bangalore, Calcutta and Madras, he added.

From Germany, air cargo to India is a traditional mix of industrial machinery, electronics and pharmaceutical goods, he said. "From India, cargo is still mostly textiles but we are starting to see more computer parts," he noted.
